question: What is the most important dry fly fishing skill to develop?
answer: Drift — achieving and maintaining a drag-free presentation from the moment the fly lands until it lifts off. Watch the foam bubbles and debris on the surface — your fly must travel at exactly the same speed as the current it sits in. Begin with short drifts close to you where you can observe clearly, then extend distance as your mending and leader control improve. No pattern will compensate for a dragging fly — ever.

question: What dry fly patterns work best in the Smoky Mountains?
answer: CDC Klinkhammers and CDC comparaduns riding half in and half out of the film consistently fool selective trout that refuse fully floating patterns. Spinner patterns — especially rusty spinners and CDC spent wings in sizes 16-22 — are the most overlooked and most productive dry fly situation on Smoky Mountain streams. Traditional parachutes, elk hair caddis, and Wulff patterns remain productive on faster broken water. In summer carry ants, beetles, and hoppers in multiple sizes.

question: How do I net a dry fly trout without dropping it?
answer: Never reel frantically when a fish is close — the rod tip vibrates up and down creating slack and dropped fish. Mac Brown rarely uses the reel even on large trout. Instead send the fish airborne to the net or hydroplane it across the surface on final approach. Keep the rod high and tight throughout. The moment you reach for the net with your off hand is when most fish are lost — the shoulder dips, the rod drops, and slack enters the system.

question: When should I use active versus passive dry fly presentations?
answer: Passive presentations — dead drift at the speed of the current — are correct for mayflies and spent spinners that ride motionless in the film. Active presentations — a skate, skitter, or hop — are correct for caddis and stoneflies whose natural behavior is erratic movement on the surface. Reading rise forms tells you which to use: a sipping rise means passive, a splashy aggressive rise means active. When in doubt, start passive and introduce movement only if fish are refusing a dead drift.

question: What equipment is best for dry fly fishing in the Smokies?
answer: A 9-foot 4-weight rod with a medium action is the ideal all-around dry fly tool for Smoky Mountain streams — light enough to feel the cast at short range and flexible enough to protect fine tippet on the strike. A 12-16 foot Maxima Chameleon leader tapering to 6X or 7X fluorocarbon tippet. Frogs Fanny or Dry Magic for fly floatation. Fullers earth and glycerin mud to sink the tippet section. CDC oil for emerger and film patterns. Polarized glasses to read rise forms and spot fish.
